clue.text: The case is soaked, and everything inside

indicators.note: inside tells us the word for everything sits within the word for soaked

parts.note: soaked means wet
everything means all

explanation.surface: A suitcase left out in the rain is drenched, contents and all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts ALL within WET. 'The case' is a case for banknotes, not luggage.
explanation.definitionFit: A pocket case for holding money and cards is a synonym.

clue.text: Romeo and Juliet take notes. That's the story

definitions.text: Romeo and Juliet take notes. That's the story

parts.words: Romeo and Juliet take notes. That's the story
parts.note: Shakespeare's lovers retold as a musical, with songs added, whose title ends in the word story

explanation.surface: The young lovers are writing things down to get their tale straight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take notes' means set to music: the Bernstein musical moves the plot of Romeo and Juliet to New York, and its title ends with 'Story'.
explanation.definitionFit: The first half of the title of the 1957 Broadway musical that retells Shakespeare's tragedy in Manhattan.

clue.text: How to have a clean-up from Arundel ?

indicators.note: from here means made out of, so the letters of the town are reworked

explanation.surface: Someone asks how to tidy up after a visit to Arundel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' tells you to make the answer from the letters of ARUNDEL, a town in Sussex, southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: To wash clothes is to clean them; the word also means to clean up dirty money.

parts.note: an Anglo-Saxon monarch whose name begins with a woman's name, then a man's

explanation.surface: A gallant monarch brings in the rule that women go first.
explanation.walkthrough: The name puts a lady's name, ETHEL, first, followed by a man's, BERT. He was the king of Kent baptised by St Augustine.
explanation.definitionFit: An Anglo-Saxon king of Kent, the first English ruler to become a Christian.

explanation.surface: Someone wants their dessert arranged neatly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Afters' is British slang for the dessert course.
explanation.definitionFit: Apple-pie order is an idiom for perfect tidiness, and a fruit pastry pudding is a typical British dessert, which Britons call afters.

clue.text: That quick prowl perhaps to find cover

indicators.note: perhaps hints the words could be something else, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cat on a fast nighttime prowl looks for somewhere to hide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges all fourteen letters of THAT QUICK PROWL.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedspread sewn from scraps of fabric is a covering for a bed.

clue.text: This pool holds a multitude of people

definitions.text: This pool holds a multitude of people

parts.words: This pool holds a multitude of people
parts.note: put this word before pool and you have a large English port city full of people

explanation.surface: A swimming pool crammed with bathers.
explanation.walkthrough: Add the answer to 'pool' and you get Liverpool, a big city; the clue reads the place name as 'answer pool'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bodily organ whose name, set before pool, names a populous English city.

clue.text: A grain of foot trouble for Father?

parts.note: pop is an informal word for father
a corn is a painful patch of hard skin on the foot

explanation.surface: Dad has a small ailment of the feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for Father' reads as a possession, but POP is just the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Maize kernels that puff up when heated form a snack grain.

parts.note: the final phase of a chess game, read as its end, a conclusion

explanation.surface: A chess game reaches a desperate position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In extremis' means in dire straits, but here at the extremity: the end of the game.
explanation.definitionFit: A conclusion or finish, as in the endgame of chess.

parts.note: not literary figures but people who write letters to one another, or reporters

explanation.surface: Literary figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Men of letters' suggests authors and scholars, but means letter-writers or newspaper reporters.
explanation.definitionFit: People who exchange mail, or journalists who report from abroad, are writers of letters.

parts.note: a seaside town that lies north of Liverpool yet is named for the opposite compass point plus a word for a harbour, haven

explanation.surface: A nickname locals use for a northern harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: The town lies north of Liverpool on the Lancashire coast, so for Liverpudlians its 'south' name really means a northern haven.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lancashire resort town north of Liverpool, whose name pairs a compass point with a harbour.

indicators.note: hearted says the soft letter becomes the heart, placed in the middle of the rest
uncommonly signals the letters of diva arranged in an unusual way

parts.note: P, piano, is the musical marking for soft

explanation.surface: A gentle-natured opera singer sings unusually off-key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommonly' rearranges DIVA to VAID, and 'hearted' puts P at its centre. 'Flat' is a musical word in the surface, but here means dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Insipid, lifeless talk or writing is flat, lacking spirit.

clue.text: He's no better, putting something on a horse

definitions.text: He's no better, putting something on a horse

parts.words: He's no better, putting something on a horse
parts.note: the person who puts something on a horse is not a gambler placing a bet but a craftsman whose leather seat goes on its back

explanation.surface: A punter who wagers on a horse does no better than anyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'better' is one who bets; 'putting something on a horse' sounds like a wager but means fitting a saddle.
explanation.definitionFit: A leatherworker who makes horses' seats and harness puts his product on the animal, not money.

clue.text: Noted Marxist gets on, on Ahab's ship

parts.note: Harpo was one of the Marx Brothers, the famous comedy team
taken as written

explanation.surface: A well-known communist boards Captain Ahab's vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marxist' points to the Marx Brothers, not politics. The definition names where the answer is found: Ahab hunts the whale in Moby-Dick.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbed whaling spear is the weapon carried aboard the Pequod in Melville's novel.

clue.text: Mournful numbers composed by a half-hearted digger

indicators.note: composed means put together anew, so the remaining letters are rearranged
half-hearted means the double letter at the word's heart is cut to one

explanation.surface: A gloomy gravedigger writes some sad verses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-hearted' drops one of the two central Gs from DIGGER, giving DIGER, which 'composed' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A lament sung at a funeral is a set of sorrowful verses, numbers being songs.

clue.text: This yard is not located here

definitions.text: This yard is not located here

parts.words: This yard is not located here
parts.note: the London police headquarters is named after a northern country, though it stands nowhere near it

explanation.surface: A garden or courtyard is said to be elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotland Yard is the headquarters of London's Metropolitan Police, in London, not in the country it names.
explanation.definitionFit: The Metropolitan Police base bears the name of the country but sits in London.

clue.text: With love from the gods ? Not this

definitions.text: With love from the gods ? Not this

parts.words: With love from the gods ? Not this
parts.note: the proverb says those whom the gods love die young, so they never get a long life

explanation.surface: A message signed off with affection from on high.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'Whom the gods love dies young' (Menander) means a long life is the one gift the gods' favourites miss.
explanation.definitionFit: A long lifespan is what the proverb denies to the gods' favourites.

parts.note: introductory pieces of music played before a larger work

explanation.surface: Things that open a show.
explanation.walkthrough: These are pieces that open a work, like an overture before the curtain rises.
explanation.definitionFit: Short introductory pieces of music come before the main work, as an opening act does.

parts.note: to fret is to worry, but ornamental woodcarving with a fine saw also takes its name from the same word

explanation.surface: A job that need not cause anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: Fret here is the decorative pattern cut with a fretsaw, not anxiety.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornamental openwork cut in thin wood is a craft hobby, with no anxiety involved.

clue.text: Fain would he climb, yet feared he to fall

definitions.text: Fain would he climb, yet feared he to fall

parts.words: Fain would he climb, yet feared he to fall
parts.note: recasts the line an Elizabethan courtier scratched on a window, 'Fain would I climb, yet fear I to fall'

explanation.surface: An ambitious man longs to rise but fears falling.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Walter Raleigh wrote the line on a window pane; Queen Elizabeth I replied 'If thy heart fails thee, climb not at all'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Elizabethan courtier and explorer who wrote that line about ambition.

parts.note: fill in the missing word of the line from A. A. Milne's poem The King's Breakfast

explanation.surface: A quotation from a children's poem with its last word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: In The King's Breakfast the queen suggests marmalade instead of butter, because many people find it more pleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's word is a comparative meaning more pleasant, completing the line about marmalade.

parts.note: a caretaker already takes care, so telling him to take care is wasted

explanation.surface: A janitor gets a pointless word of advice.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a warning to take care, wasted on someone whose job title says he takes care.
explanation.definitionFit: A word of warning urging someone to be careful.

clue.text: Girl shows what she can get with publicity backing

parts.note: what a girl can get is a man, a husband or boyfriend

indicators.note: backing means the word for publicity is turned round to run backwards

parts.note: an ad is an advertisement, publicity

explanation.surface: A young woman reveals what she can win with a bit of advertising support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns AD into DA, which follows A MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name, so an example of a girl's name.

parts.note: a pale shade of red can be described as a soft red, which also reads as a woman's first name

explanation.surface: Pink Lady is a cocktail or an apple variety.
explanation.walkthrough: Pink is a mild red; joined up, those two words give a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name that splits into words meaning gentle and crimson, a description of pink.

indicators.note: two-way says the word reads the same whichever way it is taken

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: An astronomer who scans the sky in both directions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two-way' tells you the answer reads the same forwards and backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An electronic detection system scanning the air for aircraft keeps watch over the sky.

parts.note: a peer is an equal, so someone who does not count as one is the negative of that; it also means not up to a task

explanation.surface: Someone is refused a seat in the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' suggests a lord, but here it means an equal; 'unequal to' also means not capable of.
explanation.definitionFit: Being not up to a job, or not on a level with another, is the sense of lacking parity.

indicators.note: madly signals the letters of the name are thrown into a crazy new order

explanation.surface: Diana is having a wild time swimming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'madly' rearranges DIANA. The definition describes the answer as a creature found in the water.
explanation.definitionFit: A water nymph of Greek myth lives in rivers and springs, always swimming.

parts.note: something that has been reduced to nothing, cancelled out or voided

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a matter as unimportant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made nothing of' sounds like shrugging something off, but means literally turned into nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cancelled or rendered void has been reduced to zero effect.

clue.text: A metaphor is mixed but the content is pithy

definitions.note: an adjective standing for a noun: the answer is a pithy saying

indicators.note: the content of the phrase means letters held within it, running across the words

explanation.surface: A writer mixes metaphors but still says something terse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the content' picks the letters inside 'metaphor is mixed'. The definition is loose: a pithy saying, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A short, memorable maxim is the very model of terse expression.

parts.note: animals in the wild whose cry sounds like laughing

explanation.surface: Things that make people roar with mirth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' sounds like uncontrolled, but means in the wild: these African scavengers have a cackling call.
explanation.definitionFit: African scavenging carnivores famed for a cackling call that resembles a laugh.
